docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Do any imports hint at what this malware does? If so, which imports are they?

  • Lab01-01.dll

The imported functions suggest that the sample may establish a network connection to a remote host, send and receive data, create or manage additional processes, delay its execution using time APIs, and ensure that only one instance of itself is running using mutex APIs. However, these are only assumptions based on the imported functions and require further analysis to confirm.

  • Lab01-01.exe

CreateFileA, FindFirstFileA, FindNextFileA, and CopyFileA suggest that the sample may create files, search for files, and copy files on the system.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Are there any other files or host-based indicators that you could look for on infected systems?

  • Lab01-01.exe

The CopyFileA function may copy Lab01-01.dll to C:\Windows\System32\kerne132.dll. Therefore, executing the sample may infect the system. Additionally, there is an interesting string: WARNING_THIS_WILL_DESTROY_YOUR_MACHINE.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
What network-based indicators could be used to find this malware on infected machines?

  • Lab01-01.dll

In Lab01-01.dll, the IP address 127.26.152.13 may be used by the infected machine to communicate with a remote host by sending and receiving data. Therefore, monitoring network traffic for connections to this IP address may help identify infected machines.

From the section headers, we can tell that the file is packed because there is a significant difference between the Raw Size and the Virtual Size. This indicates that the executable unpacks itself during execution.

Another indicator is the small number of imported functions, along with the presence of LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress, which are commonly used by packers to resolve imports at runtime.

docs.title: My notes for chapter 1
docs.text:
Import by Ordinal

The file Lab01-01.dll imports functions from WS2_32.dll by ordinal instead of by name, which can make static analysis more difficult.

The 8 represents the IMAGE_ORDINAL_FLAG (MSB = 1), indicating that the Windows loader should import the function by its ordinal value rather than by its name. The remaining bits are simply used to store the ordinal value.

However, when the file is opened in IDA, the ordinal imports are automatically resolved to their corresponding function names:

docs.title: Important APIs
docs.text:
• CreateMutexA: Creates or opens a named or unnamed mutex object.
  • OpenMutexW: Opens an existing named mutex object.
  • GetModuleFileNameA: Retrieves the fully qualified path for the file that contains the specified module. The module must have been loaded by the current process.
  • OpenSCManagerA: Establishes a connection to the service control manager on the specified computer and opens the specified service control manager database.
  • CreateServiceA: Creates a service object and adds it to the specified service control manager database.
  • StartServiceCtrlDispatcherA: Connects the main thread of a service process to the service control manager, which causes the thread to be the service control dispatcher thread for the calling process.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Use the Imports window to browse to gethostbyname. Where is the import located?

The import is located at address 0x100163CC.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
How many functions call gethostbyname?

There are 18 cross-references shown for gethostbyname, but there are only 9 actual call sites. This is because IDA displays two references for each imported function call through the IAT: a procedure reference (p) for the call itself and a read reference (r) because the call reads the function pointer from the Import Address Table (IAT). Thus, each call ds:gethostbyname appears twice in the xrefs list, even though it represents a single call instruction.

Looking at the xrefs, we can see that gethostbyname is called from only in **7 different functions: - sub_10001074:loc_100011AF - sub_10001074+1D3 - sub_10001074+26B - sub_10001365:loc_100014A0 - sub_10001656+101 - sub_1000208F+3A1 - sub_10002CCE+4F7

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Focusing on the call to gethostbyname located at 0x10001757, can you fig-ure out which DNS request will be made?

The string stored in memory is: [This is RDO]pics.practicalmalwareanalysis.com

The code adds 0x0D to the string pointer, skipping the prefix: pics.practicalmalwareanalysis.com

This is the hostname passed to gethostbyname, so it is the DNS request that will be made.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text:
Use the Strings window to locate the string \cmd.exe /c in the disassembly. Where is it located?

The string is located at address: 0x10095B34

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
What is happening in the area of code that references \cmd.exe /c?

The string has a single cross-reference.

Following this cross reference,it retrieves the Windows system directory and constructs the command interpreter path. Depending on the operating system, it uses either cmd.exe /c or command.exe /c. The /c switch instructs the interpreter to execute the supplied command and terminate afterward.

It continuously receives commands from the remote client over the socket connection. Incoming bytes are assembled into a command string stored in Buf1

It first checks whether the received command is one of its built-in commands. If a match is found, it executes the corresponding internal function. Otherwise, the command is handled by the Windows command interpreter cmd.exe /c

And these strings identify the malware's remote shell and display session information before processing commands.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text:
In the same area, at 0x100101C8, it looks like dword_1008E5C4 is a global variable that helps decide which path to take. How does the malware set dword_1008E5C4? (Hint: Use dword_1008E5C4’s cross-references.)

Examining the cross-references to dword_1008E5C4, we find three references. One of them writes to the variable, while the other two only read it.

The write reference assigns the return value of sub_10003695 to dword_1008E5C4.

Analyzing sub_10003695 shows that it calls GetVersionExA.

GetVersionExA fills an OSVERSIONINFOA structure. The function compares VersionInformation.dwPlatformId against 2, which corresponds to the Windows NT platform.

On the NT windows platform the value of dwPlatformId is 2.

If the comparison succeeds, setz al sets AL to 1, otherwise, it returns 0.

Therefore, dword_1008E5C4 stores whether the operating system belongs to the Windows NT family.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text:
A few hundred lines into the subroutine at 0x1000FF58, a series of com-parisons use memcmp to compare strings. What happens if the string compar-ison to robotwork is successful (when memcmp returns 0)?

If memcmp returns 0, the malware calls sub_100052A2.

This function opens a registry key and retrieves the registry value named WorkTime.

It converts the value to an integer using atoi, formats it with sprintf, and passes it to sub_100038EE.

The same steps are repeated for the registry value WorkTimes, after which the registry key is closed.

docs.title: Q11
docs.text:
What does the export PSLIST do?

The function first sets dword_1008E5BC to 1, then calls sub_100036C3.

sub_100036C3 performs several checks and returns either 0 or 1. If the value of dwPlatformId is 2, and the value of dwMajorVersion is greater than 5 it will return 1, else it will return 0.

The value of dwMajorVersion is greater than 5 from Windows Vista and above.

If the return value is 0, PSLISTfunction immediately returns 0x16.

docs.title: Q14
docs.text:
At 0x10001358, there is a call to Sleep (an API function that takes one parameter containing the number of milliseconds to sleep). Looking backward through the code, how long will the program sleep if this code executes?

The string: [This is CTI]30 is adjusted by adding 0x0D, producing: 30 Then: 

atoi("30") = 30
30 × 1000 = 30000 ms

Therefore, the malware sleeps for 30 seconds.

docs.title: Q17
docs.text:
Search for usage of the in instruction (opcode 0xED). This instruction is used with a magic string VMXh to perform VMware detection. Is that in use in this malware? Using the cross-references to the function that executes the in instruction, is there further evidence of VMware detection?

Searching for the 0xED opcode reveals the following instruction:

The in eax, dx instruction reads 32 bits from the I/O port specified in dx. In this case, however, it is used as part of the VMware backdoor detection technique. The code loads the magic value 'VMXh' into eax, sets dx to the VMware I/O port ('VX'), and executes the in instruction.

If the program is running inside VMware, the hypervisor responds by placing 'VMXh' into ebx, causing the comparison to succeed.

Further evidence of VMware detection is the string: text Found Virtual Machine, Install Cancel.

which is referenced by the detection routine. If a virtual machine is detected, the malware displays this message and cancels the installation.

docs.title: Q19
docs.text:
If you have the IDA Python plug-in installed (included with the com-mercial version of IDA Pro), run Lab05-01.py, an IDA Pro Python script provided with the malware for this book. (Make sure the cursor is at 0x1001D988.) What happens after you run the script?

The original script uses ScreenEA(), which did not work in my case, so I modified it to use idc.here() instead.

# sea = ScreenEA()

# for i in range(0x00,0x50):
#         b = Byte(sea+i)

#         PatchByte(sea+i,decoded_byte)

import idautils 
import idaapi

sea = idc.here()

for i in range(0x00,0x50):
    b = ord(idaapi.get_bytes(sea+i, 1))
    decoded_byte = b ^ 0x55
    ida_bytes.patch_byte(sea+i,decoded_byte)

Running the script xor decodes the data, converting it into readable strings.

docs.title: Q21
docs.text:
Open the script with a text editor. How does it work?

The script decodes an xor encoded data block at the current cursor location in IDA.

It first gets the current address using idc.here(). Then, it loops through the next 0x50 bytes, reading each byte with idaapi.get_bytes(). Each byte is xored with the constant 0x55, and the decoded byte is written back into the database using ida_bytes.patch_byte().

As a result, the encrypted data is replaced with its decoded form, making the hidden strings readable in IDA.

The decoding algorithm is: decoded_byte = encoded_byte ^ 0x55

docs.text:
What can this function do?

The function subtracts the ASCII value of 'a' from the command character returned by the previous function. This determines which entry in the jump table will be executed. If the character is outside the expected range (a–e), the program prints: Error 3.2: Not a valid command provided

If the character is a, which mean its ascii value is 97 it will jump to this case:

It creats a directory, its name and path is: C:\\Temp

If the character is b, which mean its asccii value is 98 it will jump to this case:

It copies the existing file name to C:\\Temp\\cc.exe

If the character is c, which mean its asccii value is 99 it will jump to this case:

It deletes the file C:\\Temp\\cc.exe

If the character is d, which mean its asccii value is100` it will jump to this case:

It opens the HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run registry key and creates or updates a REG_SZ value named Malware with the path C:\Temp\cc.exe to achieve persistence by executing the malware at Windows startup/logon.

If it faild, it will print "Error 3.1: Could not set Registry value"

If the character is e, which mean its asccii value is101` it will jump to this case:

It sleeps for 0x186A0 milliseconds (100 seconds).

docs.title: Q2

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
What is the difference between this lab’s parse HTML function and those of the previous labs?

The User-Agent string is different from the previous labs. It appends the value of arg_0 to the User-Agent string.

arg_0 receives the value of var_C, which is passed as the first argument to the function.

As a result, each iteration uses a different User-Agent string.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
How long will this program run? (Assume that it is connected to the Internet.)

The loop will run for 0x5A0 time, and in every time it sleeps for 0x0EA60 milliseconds. This mean it will take (0x5A0 * 0x0EA60) milliseconds, which equal to 86400000 milliseconds, or 1440 in minutes, or 1 day

The loop executes 0x5A0 (1440) times. During each iteration, the program sleeps for 0xEA60 (60,000 milliseconds).

Therefore, the total execution time is: - 0x5A0 × 0xEA60 = 86,400,000 milliseconds - 1,440 minutes - 24 hours (1 day)

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
What is the purpose of this malware?

The malware first checks whether the system has an active Internet connection.

If a connection is available, it enters a loop that runs for approximately 24 hours.

During each iteration, it downloads a command from the remote server, extracts a command character from the HTML response, and executes the corresponding action through the switch table introduced in Lab 6-3.

My notes while solving this phase

[rbp+4] = first     [0, 14]

func(first, 0, 14) == 10

---

[rbp+108] = arg2
[rbp+110] = arg3
[rbp+100] = arg1

15 => 7 => 3 => 5

6 + 5 + 3 + 7 = 21 = 0x15
7 + 3 = 10 = 0xa

docs.title: First solution
docs.text:
If we enter func4

If the value of midpoint is equal to the first argument

If the value of midpoint is less than the first argument

If the value of midpoint is more than the first argument

I entered "5 10" to trace the program and this is what I found:

When reached ret instruction the value in eax is same as the input

Then it returns to the previous ret address which pushed on the stack

And adds to it the value of last midpoint

So, we entered 5 it added to it : 7+ 3, which is 15, 0xF

The function adds the sum of midpoints to your input.

The used equation in the code:

cmp = ((arg3 - arg2) / 2) + arg2
which is equal to:
(arg3 + arg2) / 2

first midpoint = (0 + 14) / 2 = 7 second midpoint = (0 + 7) / 2 = 3 third midpoint = (3 + 7) / 2 = 5 now, we reached 5, so it returns 5 + 3 + 7 = 0xF

To get the value 10, we need to enter 3, 7 + 3 = 10

If you want to understand recursive functions more, check my article on Recursive Functions in Assembly.

docs.title: Another solution
docs.text:
I also traced the program and wrote this python burte force script:

def phase_4():
    if (myInput > 0) and (myInput <= 14):
        x = func_4(myInput, 0, 14)
        if (x == 10):
            print(f"win , input = {myInput}")
        else:
            print(f"fail , input = {myInput}")


def func_4(myInput, num2, num3):
    cmp = num2 + ((num3 - num2) >> 1)   # 7

    if (cmp <= myInput):

        if (cmp >= myInput):
            return cmp

        return (cmp + func_4(myInput, cmp+1, num3))

    else:

        return (cmp + func_4(myInput, num2, cmp-1))

for i in range(14):
    myInput = i+1
    phase_4()

so, input is: 3 10

docs.title: Analyzing a Single Node
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

typedef struct Node
{
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

int main()
{
    Node node;

    node.value = 10;
    node.next = NULL;

    return 0;
}

The assembly does not clearly indicate that a structure is being used. The compiler simply writes values to memory, just as it would for ordinary local variables.

One small clue is that the second member begins at [rbp+10h] instead of [rbp+0Ch]. This is because the compiler inserted four bytes of padding after the int member so that the pointer is aligned on an 8-byte boundary.

However, this alone is not enough to conclude that the object is a linked list—or even a structure. From the assembly alone, we only know that there is a 4-byte value followed by an 8-byte value.

We can't identify a linked list from a single instruction or a single object. Instead, we recognize the overall pattern created by pointer dereferences, traversal loops, and NULL termination. We will see these patterns in the following examples.

When the program is compiled with debug information (PDB), ida can recover the structure definition and display the member names and offsets.

docs.title: Analyzing Multiple Nodes
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct Node
{
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

int main()
{
    Node *head = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    Node *second = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    Node *third = malloc(sizeof(Node));

    head->value = 10;
    head->next = second;

    second->value = 20;
    second->next = third;

    third->value = 30;
    third->next = NULL;

    Node *cur = head;

    while (cur)
    {
        printf("%d\n", cur->value);
        cur = cur->next;
    }

    free(head);
    free(second);
    free(third);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: You can recognize the linked lists, if the code meets: - Accessing the first field ([reg]). - Accessing the pointer field ([reg+8]). - Repeated pointer dereference. - A loop ending when the pointer becomes NULL.

docs.title: Recursive Functions in Assembly (x64dbg)
docs.text: I wrote two simple programs in c, compiled them, and traced their execution in x64dbg to understand how recursive functions works in assembly.

docs.title: Recursive Functions Without a Return Value (void)
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

void func(int n)
{
    if (n == 0)
        return;

    printf("%d\n", n);

    func(n - 1);
}

int main()
{
    func(3);
}

The function prints the current value of n, decrements it by one, and recursively calls itself until n becomes zero. Since the function's return type is void, it does not return a value to its caller.

The main function calls the func and sends to it the value 3

after the call instruction, the caller does not use the value in eax. Although eax may contain a value left by previous instructions or function calls, the caller ignores it because a void function does not return a meaningful value.

When a function calls another function, the CPU pushes the return address onto the stack and creates a new stack frame for the callee.

The same behavior occurs when a function calls itself recursively. Every recursive call creates its own independent stack frame and stores its own return address on the stack.

Once the base case is reached, the recursive calls begin to return. Each ret instruction pops the corresponding return address from the stack and transfers execution back to the instruction immediately following the call instruction in the previous stack frame. This process continues until all recursive calls have returned.

docs.title: Recursive Functions With a Return Value
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

int func(int n)
{
    if (n == 0)
        return 1;

    return n * func(n - 1);
}

int main()
{
    printf("%d\n", func(3));

    return 0;
}

The function recursively calls itself until it reaches the base case (n == 0), where it returns 1.

Once the base case is reached, the recursive calls stop. The program then begins stack unwinding. Each ret instruction returns execution to the instruction immediately following the corresponding call.

In this example, execution returns to address 0x00007FF613F218CE. At this point, the caller uses the return value from the previous recursive call to compute its own return value. This process repeats until all recursive calls have returned.

The return value of each recursive call is stored in rax. The caller then uses this value to perform the multiplication before returning to its caller.
